item.title: Predictive performance of bedside physiological parameters for the failure of prophylactic non-invasive ventilation after extubation
item.description:
Background: Extubation failure is associated with increased mortality. Whether bedside physiological variables can identify patients at risk of reintubation during prophylactic NIV after extubation is unknown.

Methods: In this post hoc analysis of a multicenter physiological study, 60 hypoxemic adults at high risk of extubation failure underwent two 1-hour NIV sessions after planned extubation, with oronasal and full-face masks in randomized crossover order. We assessed the magnitude of airway occlusion pressure (Pocc), the esophageal pressure swing (ΔPes), SpO₂/FiO₂, respiratory rate, tidal volume, dynamic lung elastance (EL,dyn), ROX index [(SpO₂/FiO₂)/respiratory rate] and the pressure-oxygenation index (POX, SpO₂/FiO₂ divided by Pocc). Prophylactic NIV failure was reintubation for respiratory failure within 7 days. Discrimination was assessed by ROC analysis.

Results: Fourteen patients (23%) experienced NIV failure. Pocc yielded areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.83 (95% CI, 0.71-0.95) with the oronasal mask and 0.83 (95% CI, 0.72-0.95) with the full-face mask, showing greater discriminative performance than tidal volume (AUCs, 0.55 and 0.53), respiratory rate (0.54 and 0.38), SpO₂/FiO₂ (0.51 and 0.50), and the ROX index (0.54 and 0.38; all p < 0.05). By contrast, the discriminative performance of Pocc did not differ from that of EL,dyn (AUCs, 0.72 and 0.73; p = 0.08 and 0.11), POX (AUCs, 0.82 and 0.81; p = 0.68 and 0.29), or |ΔPes| (AUCs, 0.83 and 0.82; p = 1.00 and 0.64).

Conclusions: During prophylactic NIV, Pocc discriminated NIV failure better than conventional bedside variables, with no detectable difference from directly measured inspiratory effort. External validation is required.

item.title: Discordant evidence on corticosteroids in sepsis: a meta-research study
item.description:
Background: Despite an extensive evidence base of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and systematic reviews (SRs), current sepsis guidelines provide only weak recommendations for corticosteroid therapy, while available SRs report conflicting mortality conclusions. We aimed to characterize the evidence landscape of SRs evaluating corticosteroids for sepsis, including their clinical scope, underlying RCT evidence bases, mortality conclusions, and to explore potential sources of discordance.

Methods: Meta-research study of SRs on corticosteroids in sepsis published between 2015 and 2025. Study-pool overlap was assessed using a SR×RCT inclusion matrix, Jaccard similarity (J), and hierarchical clustering. SRs and RCTs were classified according to standardized Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome (PICO) profiles. We explored discordance in short-term mortality conclusions among clinically comparable SRs and potential associations with study-pool composition, target populations, and methodological characteristics.

Results: Forty-two SRs including 121 unique RCTs were identified. More than half of pairwise SR comparisons shared no RCTs, and only three pairs showed high overlap (J > 0.8). SRs addressing similar intervention and target population profiles frequently relied on different study pools. Among 38 SRs with short-term mortality meta-analyses, 15 (39%) reported benefit and 23 (61%) no evidence of effect. Discordance occurred exclusively among SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies; conclusions were consistent for hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone (benefit) and hydrocortisone, ascorbic acid, and thiamine (no evidence of effect). SRs including adult sepsis ± shock populations more frequently reported benefit than those restricted to septic shock (62% vs 22%), although this comparison was based on only 22 SRs evaluating broad, non-specific corticosteroid strategies and estimates were imprecise. No single methodological or clinical factor consistently explained discordance.

Conclusions: SRs addressing apparently similar clinical questions frequently synthesized different underlying evidence bases and reported discordant conclusions. When selecting SRs to inform clinical decisions and recommendations for sepsis management, clinicians and guideline developers should consider not only methodological quality and reported PICO, but also whether the included RCTs adequately represent the intended clinical question.

item.title: BEYOND PICS: a conceptual framework for post-ICU recovery stewardship
item.description:
As survival from critical illness improves, the global burden of post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) and PICS-family continues to grow, reshaping the goals of modern intensive care. Despite growing awareness, prevention, follow-up and rehabilitation remain fragmented, and important gaps persist in the organisation of recovery-oriented care. We propose BEYOND PICS, a conceptual framework for ICU survivorship built around six complementary pillars: Begin before ICU discharge, Early follow-up and equitable access, Your journey, Ongoing multidomain assessment and rehabilitation, Networked care, and Driving improvement. Rather than describing clinical interventions to be implemented in practice, the framework promotes a coordinated recovery pathway integrating prevention, patient partnership, education, rehabilitation, multidisciplinary collaboration and continuous quality improvement across the peri-ICU continuum. BEYOND PICS is not a clinical bundle or guideline, it provides a mental model to guide the organization of care, integrating the key components of ICU survivorship into a coherent continuum of care while highlighting priorities for future research.

item.title: Family members' experiences of death and organ donation in intensive and critical care units: a qualitative systematic review with thematic synthesis
item.description:
Family members of patients in intensive care units (ICUs) occupy a uniquely distressing position, navigating death determination and organ donation decisions at the most acute moments of loss. Qualitative evidence on these experiences has predominantly focused on donation after brain death (DBD), leaving the distinctive challenges of donation after circulatory death (DCD) largely unexplored, with no synthesis to date attending to both pathways within a single review. This review aimed to synthesise qualitative evidence on family members' experiences of death determination and organ donation in intensive and critical care settings across both DBD and DCD pathways. Thematic synthesis was employed, incorporating reciprocal translation from meta-ethnography and constant comparison from grounded theory, following the Thomas and Harden three-stage analytical framework. Reporting adhered to the Enhancing Transparency in Reporting the Synthesis of Qualitative Research (ENTREQ) guidelines. Five databases were searched in December 2025 with no date restriction. Eligible studies were peer-reviewed qualitative or mixed-methods publications reporting verbatim family member accounts of death determination or organ donation in adult ICU settings. Quality was appraised using the CASP checklist and the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT). Twenty-eight studies (2001-2025; 14 countries) were included. Of the 28 studies, 13 addressed DBD exclusively, four addressed DCD exclusively, and eight examined both pathways. Three analytical themes emerged. "Constructing Death" pertains to how families make sense of death determination through suspended temporality, bodily witnessing, and contested definitions, processes differing markedly between pathways. "The Contested Body" encompasses tensions between bodily sanctity and organ donation, shaped by clinician behaviours and consent processes. "Relational Meaning-Making" regards how families construct meaning through collective deliberation, cultural and religious frameworks, and farewell rituals. Whilst both pathways share core experiential dimensions, DBD families navigated the sensory dissonance of a physiologically supported yet neurologically dead loved one, whilst DCD families faced temporal compression and the moral weight of perceived involvement in an irreversible clinical event. Family experiences are simultaneously individual, relational, and culturally embedded. Findings point to context-sensitive practice considerations, communication quality, person-centred care, and institutional flexibility, that may support families across both DBD and DCD contexts.

item.title: A pilot study of circulating DPP3 and renin to identify high-risk phenotypes and mortality in septic shock
item.description:
Sepsis and septic shock are life-threatening conditions associated with high mortality and limited treatment options. Rapid identification of patients at risk for worse outcomes and/or targeted therapeutics are needed. Elevated levels of renin and dipeptidyl peptidase 3 (DPP3) individually have been associated with increased risk in septic shock, which may reflect an attenuated Angiotensin II response as DPP3 contributes to the metabolism of Angiotensin II. We applied an approach to distinguish both circulating renin and DPP3 concentrations at their clinically relevant threshold values for risk in septic shock patients of ≥ 180 pg/mL and ≥ 40 ng/mL, respectively. This analysis revealed four clinical phenotypes of patients with low risk (low renin/low DPP3), intermediate risk (high renin/low DPP3 or low renin/high DPP3) and those patients with the highest risk (high renin/high DPP3). We conclude that the subclassification of both circulating renin and DPP3 concentrations may better identify those patients at greater risk and inform more optimal treatment approaches.

item.title: CT-based radiomics for interpretable outcome prediction after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: a multicenter cohort study
item.description:
Background: Prognostic assessment after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) mainly relies on clinical variables and computed tomography (CT) findings, but current models often lack biological interpretability. We developed and validated a clinical-radiomics prognostic model and subsequently performed exploratory cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic characterization of model-defined risk phenotypes.

Methods: This multicenter cohort from the PROSAH-MPC registry included 879 patients across four hospitals. Patients from the primary center were split into training (n = 637) and internal validation (n = 160) cohorts, while patients from three other centers formed an external validation cohort (n = 82). Admission CT hemorrhagic lesions were automatically segmented using the validated BrainHemoAI platform, and radiomic features were extracted with PyRadiomics. Clinical, radiomics, and combined clinical-radiomics XGBoost models were developed and interpreted using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Risk scores from the clinical-radiomics model were applied to an independent prospective enrichment, gene setCSF​ proteomic cohort to define combined model-based high- and low-risk groups. Gene Ontology (GO)/ Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), and protein-protein interaction (PPI) analyses were performed.

Results: The combined model yielded AUCs of 0.892 and 0.820 in the internal test and external validation cohorts, respectively. Risk reclassification analyses suggested that radiomic features may provide complementary prognostic information. SHAP identified radiomic heterogeneity and key clinical variables as major predictors. Meanwhile, exploratory CSF proteomic analysis identified candidate differentially expressed proteins and associated pathway signals that differed between groups defined by high and low combined clinical-radiomics risk scores.

Conclusions: This clinical-radiomics prognostic model enables accurate outcome prediction and provides exploratory biological insight into unfavorable recovery after aSAH, supporting refined risk stratification and potential targeted therapeutic development.

Trial registration: PROSAH-MPC. NCT05738083. Registered 16 November 2022 - Retrospectively registered, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05738083 .

item.title: Effect of megadose vitamin C in patients with sepsis: the CEMVIS randomized clinical trial
item.description:
Background: Previous randomized trials of vitamin C in sepsis have reported conflicting findings, but whether the effect of vitamin C varies according to septic shock status remains unclear. We aimed to evaluate the effect of megadose vitamin C in sepsis and explore whether treatment effect differed according to septic shock status.

Methods: CEMVIS was a multicenter, randomized, single-blind, placebo-controlled trial conducted in four tertiary hospitals in China. Adults meeting Sepsis-3 criteria were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive intravenous vitamin C (12 g every 12 h for 4 days) or placebo using stratified randomization according to septic shock status. Patients were analyzed according to the modified intention-to-treat principle. The primary outcome was 28-day mortality.

Results: Between Feb 8, 2022, and Dec 25, 2024, 114 patients in the vitamin C group and 117 in the placebo group were included in the modified intention-to-treat population. 28-day mortality did not differ significantly between groups (35/114 [30.7%] vs 36/116 [31.0%]; odds ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.56-1.74; p = 0.97). No significant differences were observed in the duration of mechanical ventilation, vasopressor therapy, and renal replacement therapy, or in changes in SOFA scores over 96 hours. Prespecified subgroup analyses showed significant interaction according to septic shock status (P for interaction = 0.026), with the treatment effects on 28-day mortality numerically favoring vitamin C among patients without septic shock (15.4% vs 34%) and numerically favoring placebo among those with septic shock (38.7% vs 29%). Hypernatremia occurred more frequently in the vitamin C group (40/114 [35.1%] vs 24/117 [20.5%]; p = 0.02). Exploratory restricted cubic spline analyses showed that increasing lactate levels were associated with a progressive shift in treatment effect from potential benefit toward potential harm. Post hoc Bayesian analyses further provided probabilistic characterization of the potential treatment effect according to septic shock status.

Conclusions: The results of this trial do not support the routine use of megadose vitamin C to reduce 28-day mortality in patients with sepsis. Treatment effects may vary according to septic shock status.

Trial registration: This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov on 3 January 2022 (identifier: NCT05194189).

item.title: Tailored strategies for vitamin C, D, iron, and carnitine in critical illness
item.description:
Background: Micronutrients are essential cofactors for metabolic, immune, and cellular processes. Low plasma concentrations are frequent in ICU patients but poorly reflect tissue stores. Inflammation drives redistribution and utilisation, while disease, reduced intake, impaired absorption, dilution, and increased losses may contribute to true deficiency. Plasma values, therefore, cannot distinguish redistribution from deficiency, making individualised requirement estimation difficult. This narrative review focuses on four micronutrients of recent high interest, aiming to address some missing links in critical illness.

Main body: Current guidelines recommend routine provision of basal micronutrient requirements for all ICU patients, with additional monitoring and increased doses reserved for high-risk groups with losses. Plasma measurements, often the only available tool, should be interpreted alongside inflammatory markers, clinical context, and risk factors. Large RCTs of vitamin C have mainly yielded neutral or negative results, which may reflect unguided supplementation across heterogeneous populations without accounting for timing, duration, dosing strategies, and biochemical formulation variability; alternatively, vitamin C may simply be ineffective as an early intervention in critical illness. Available evidence from ICU vitamin D trials indicates signals of outcome benefit, but the evidence is heterogeneous and trial sizes are limited, preventing firm ICU-specific recommendations. Ongoing large trials are expected to clarify effects of high-dose strategies. Iron status spans a narrow therapeutic window: iron deficiency and anaemia are highly prevalent during and after ICU, yet iron overload and ferroptosis-related toxicity also contribute to organ dysfunction. Targeted, hepcidin-guided intravenous (I.V.) iron therapy appears promising to safely correct deficiency. Both carnitine deficiency and high blood levels are associated with worse outcomes in ICU patients. Risk factors for alterations in carnitine concentrations include CRRT, renal and hepatic dysfunction, valproate use, inflammation, and wound losses. Supplementation should be evaluated in a stepwise approach to detect potentially excessive levels in a dose-finding RCT.

Conclusion: New biomarkers and analytical approaches are needed to differentiate redistribution from deficiency, capturing dynamic changes over time. Future approaches should move beyond plasma measurements toward cellular and functional biomarkers that better reflect stores and biological activity. Given current limitations, testing should be selective to where results are expected to alter management, include CRP, and timing guided by underlying risk. Research should prioritise precision strategies with better biomarkers and longitudinal sampling to account for dynamic risk, needs, losses, and responses.

item.title: Bacteriological profiling and antimicrobial resistance of combat-related infections: analysis of war wounds from Ukraine during 2024-2025
item.description:
Background: Combat-related wound infections in the Russo-Ukrainian war pose high morbidity due to the prevalence of multidrug-resistant (MDR) organisms. The aim of the study was to characterize pathogen distribution, antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics, and risk factors (evacuation and sampling timing) with the intent to develop a prognostic model for resistance in wounded military personnel.

Patients and methods: A retrospective analysis of 203 patients with ballistic injuries treated at a Role 3 military hospital (Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine) was performed. Microbiological sampling yielded 685 unique strains. Isolates were categorized by year (2024 vs. 2025), sampling timing (≤ 48 h vs. > 48 h), and evacuation interval (< 72 h vs. ≥ 72 h). Susceptibility testing followed EUCAST v.14-15. Bacteriological profiling was made for Multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria, Extensively Drug-Resistant (XDR), and Pan-drug-Resistant (PDR) microbes. Data was managed in WHONET Microbiology Laboratory Database Software (2025); statistical analyses used R and AMR packages. A supervised machine-learning workflow using a standard Random Forest algorithm was implemented to predict phenotypic resistance risk, with model performance evaluated by ROC-AUC analysis.

Results: Gram-negative bacteria predominated, led by A. baumannii, K. pneumoniae, E. coli, and E. cloacae. Overall resistance rate was 51.2%. True patient-level carbapenem resistance was high in K. pneumoniae (imipenem 83.1%) and A. baumannii (imipenem 91.5%); colistin retained activity. Patient-corrected MDR prevalence significantly escalated from 72.9% in 2024 to 82.3% in 2025 (p = 0.022), confirming a deepening ecological resistance reservoir. Polymicrobial infections were common (93.6% of episodes), often including MDR/XDR pathogens. Resistance was highest in the early-evacuation/early-sampling (Groups 1, 73.6% MDR) and late-evacuation/late-sampling (Groups 4, 97.1% MDR) groups. Random Forest predicted resistance with an overall AUC = 0.718, demonstrating reliable performance specifically within high-volume cohorts (Groups 1 and 4).

Conclusions: Combat wounds demonstrate a severe burden of resistant Gram-negative pathogens with stationary chronological resistance plateaus linked to evacuation and sampling timelines. The rapid colonization kinetics observed during early transit continuum indicate that the institutional reservoir is pervasive across the evacuation network. The machine-learning model provides reliable automated risk stratification for high-volume echelons to optimize empirical selection, while early clinical management must prioritize aggressive surgical debridement and source control over premature antimicrobial escalation.

item.title: Switching from controlled to assisted ventilation based on oxygenation thresholds and PEEP: a target trial emulation
item.description:
Objective: To determine whether PaO2/FiO2-based dynamic treatment strategies can optimise the timing of switching from controlled to assisted ventilation.

Design and setting: Target trial emulation using the MIMIC-IV database v3.1 (2008-2022).

Patients: Adult ICU patients on controlled invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV) for ≥ 48 h with at least one PaO2/FiO2 <300 mmHg. A sensitivity analysis included patients ventilated for ≥ 24 h, excluding post-surgical patients.

Interventions: We compared strategies defined by switching once PaO2/FiO2 exceeded predefined thresholds (150, 200, or 250 mmHg). Additionally, to account for possible PEEP-dependent effects, the thresholds were evaluated depending on the set PEEP (< 8 vs. ≥8 cmH2O), yielding nine strategies. Outcomes were 28-day restricted mean time lost (RMTL) to successful extubation (where a lower RMTL indicates a longer time to extubation) and mortality.

Measurements and main results: Among 1,635 patients, the strategy of delaying the switch until PaO2/FiO2 >250 mmHg showed a longer time to successful extubation compared to switching at > 150 mmHg or > 200 mmHg (RMTL 17.4 days [95% CI: 15.9-18.6] vs. 19.6 days [95% CI: 18.6-20.9] and 19.8 days [95% CI: 18.5-21.1], respectively). Exploratory PEEP-dependent analyses demonstrated the longest time to successful extubation with '>250 mmHg' for both low and high PEEP and the shortest with '>150 mmHg for low PEEP; >200 mmHg for high PEEP'. Among patients ventilated for ≥ 24 h, the 150 mmHg threshold was most favourable, irrespective of PEEP. No mortality differences were observed across strategies.

Conclusions: Switching as soon as PaO2/FiO2 >150 mmHg is generally favoured over delaying until > 250 mmHg. Patients requiring ≥ 48 h of controlled IMV with PEEP ≥ 8 cmH2O may potentially benefit from a slightly higher threshold (> 200 mmHg). Prospective validation is warranted.

item.title: Development and external validation of age-specific predictive models for sepsis in critically ill neonates and children using multidimensional hematological parameters: a multicenter retrospective study
item.description:
Background: Sepsis remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in neonatal and pediatric intensive care units (NICU/PICU). Given the rapid clinical deterioration of these vulnerable populations, shifting from reactive diagnosis to proactive prediction of sepsis onset is crucial. Multidimensional hematological parameters may provide new insights for risk stratification. While routine complete blood count (CBC) is widely used, the predictive potential of high-dimensional hematological cell morphology features that extend beyond traditional CBC remains under-investigated in large-scale pediatric cohorts.

Methods: This multicenter study utilized a large-scale dataset from the CALM2302 project, encompassing 17,066 critically ill neonates and children across 30 Chinese hospitals between October 2020 and October 2023. We developed population-specific CatBoost models for NICU and PICU to predict sepsis onset. To mitigate class imbalance, random undersampling was applied to the training sets. From a candidate pool of 1,924 parameters (37 routine CBC and 1,887 research features), optimized signatures of approximately 200 features were selected for each population. Model performance was evaluated by the area under the ROC curve (AUC) across internal and dual external validation cohorts. Furthermore, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was performed to ensure model interpretability and identify key biological predictors.

Results: Among the total cohort, 10,347 infants were categorized into the NICU cohort (sepsis incidence: 7.48%), while 6,719 children formed the PICU cohort (sepsis incidence: 10.92%). CatBoost was identified as the optimal architecture after benchmarking nine machine learning algorithms. The population-specific simplified 18-variable models demonstrated robust performance. In the NICU cohort, the model achieved an internal AUC of 0.846 and external AUCs of 0.742 and 0.827. For the PICU cohort, corresponding AUCs were 0.803, 0.717, and 0.811. These simplified models maintained highly comparable discriminative power to the full models (range of AUC attenuation: 0.005-0.027). SHAP analysis identified 18 key predictive features for each cohort, with only two shared features between the two populations and the remaining being cohort-specific. Notably, most of these 18 features were research parameters rather than traditional blood counts indices. Furthermore, most of these features remained statistically significant in multivariable analyses after adjustment for age, sex, and study sites.

Conclusions: In this large multicenter cohort, we developed and validated simplified 18-variable models that accurately predict sepsis in both neonatal and pediatric populations. By capturing early hematological morphological alterations beyond traditional blood counts, these models offer a robust, interpretable, and clinically accessible solution for proactive sepsis management in intensive care units.

item.title: Ventilator-circuit configurations for noninvasive ventilation in infants with acute respiratory failure: a randomized crossover trial
item.description:
Patient-ventilator synchrony may differ across ventilator and circuit configurations during noninvasive ventilation (NIV) in infants. We compared an intentional-leak single-limb turbine configuration (SLC-turbine), a dual-limb turbine configuration with an active expiratory valve (DLC-turbine), and a dual-limb compressed-gas pediatric ICU configuration (DLC-PICU) in infants receiving NIV for acute respiratory failure METHODS: In this single-center randomized crossover physiological study, infants underwent three 30-minute NIV phases in randomized order with unchanged pressure support, PEEP, and FiO₂. Esophageal pressure was used to assess the asynchrony index (AI), individual asynchronies, and inspiratory effort. Primary and secondary endpoints were AI differences between DLC-PICU and SLC-turbine and between DLC-PICU and DLC-turbine, respectively RESULTS: Twenty infants entered stabilization, 13 were randomized, and 12 completed the protocol (age 10 [7-21] months; SpO₂/FiO₂ 185 [160-220]). AI differed across configurations: 8.6% [6.7-16.5] with SLC-turbine, 25.4% [16.3-35.0] with DLC-turbine, and 45.7% [30.5-63.8] with DLC-PICU (p=0.0023). AI was higher with DLC-PICU than with SLC-turbine (Hodges-Lehmann difference +32.0%, 95% CI +13.9 to +50.1; p=0.0015) and DLC-turbine (+18.4%, 95% CI +5.9 to +36.3; p=0.021). Auto-triggering showed the clearest configuration-dependent difference and was more frequent with DLC-PICU than with SLC-turbine (7.5 [0.6-11.4] vs 0 [0-2.5] events/min; difference +5.30 events/min; p=0.0039), without a significant difference between DLC-PICU and DLC-turbine. Ineffective efforts, double triggering, and premature cycling did not differ across configurations. All NIV configurations reduced inspiratory effort versus unassisted spontaneous breathing, with no significant differences among NIV configurations CONCLUSIONS: AI was lower with SLC-turbine and DLC-turbine than with DLC-PICU and lowest with SLC-turbine. Auto-triggering showed the clearest configuration-dependent difference. All configurations reduced inspiratory effort versus unassisted spontaneous breathing, without significant between-configuration differences. Because ventilator platform, circuit and expiratory architecture, and device-specific control functions differed, effects of individual components cannot be determined. These findings are specific to the ventilators and configurations evaluated. Further studies should determine whether these physiological differences translate into improved NIV tolerance or short- and long-term clinical outcomes TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT04017780. Registered on 12 July 2019.

item.title: Impact of antibiotic prophylaxis on the occurrence of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia in trauma patients (antiVAP): a propensity score-weighted, retrospective cohort study
item.description:
Background: Short-course antibiotic prophylaxis has been associated with a reduced risk of early-onset ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) in selected populations, particularly patients with acute brain injury. However, its role in severely injured trauma patients remains controversial.

Methods: This multicentre, retrospective cohort study, conducted in 15 French trauma centres, included severely injured adults who required mechanical ventilation initiated within 24 h of admission and continued for at least 48 h. Propensity score-based analyses assessed the association between early antibiotic prophylaxis (initiated within the first 24 h of management and continued for up to 72 h) and patient outcomes. The primary outcome was early-onset VAP; secondary outcomes included late-onset VAP, extrapulmonary infections, duration of mechanical ventilation, ICU and hospital length of stay, and 30-day mortality.

Results: A total of 1,321 trauma patients were included. Antibiotic prophylaxis was administered to 746 patients (56%), with amoxicillin-clavulanic acid used in more than 90% of cases. Early-onset VAP occurred in 240 of 746 patients (32%) who received antibiotic prophylaxis and in 195 of 575 (34%) who did not. After inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with early-onset VAP (weighted odds ratio [wOR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.66-1.22; p = 0.48). A cause-specific Cox model accounting for the competing risk of death before day 7 yielded similar results (cause-specific hazard ratio [csHR] 0.87, 95% CI 0.71-1.07; p = 0.19). Antibiotic prophylaxis was not associated with improve of secondary outcomes.

Conclusions: Routine antibiotic prophylaxis in severely injured trauma patients was not associated with a reduced risk of early-onset VAP.

item.title: Acute kidney injury and renal replacement therapy: a critical synthesis of metabolic derangements and nutritional implications
item.description:
Background: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects up to 50% of critically ill patients and is frequently complicated by severe metabolic derangements, requiring the initiation of replacement therapy (RRT) in 10-15% of cases. Despite substantial progress in the diagnosis of AKI and optimisation of RRT delivery, the nutritional management of these patients remains an underexplored area.

Main body: AKI is increasingly recognised as a systemic metabolic disorder extending beyond impaired renal clearance. Key metabolic alterations include mitochondrial dysfunction, dysregulated gluconeogenesis, increased proteolysis and altered amino acid metabolism, with accelerated nitrogen wasting. These abnormalities are further amplified by acute systemic stress states, including sepsis, systemic inflammation, trauma, burns, liver dysfunction and multiorgan failure. RRT introduces additional metabolic consequences through extracorporeal losses of amino acids and micronutrients. Conversely, citrate anticoagulation, glucose-containing dialysate, and lactate-buffered solutions represent sources of clinically relevant calories. Current nutritional recommendations are largely extrapolated from heterogeneous intensive care populations. Available evidence suggests that AKI primarily influences energy balance rather than energy expenditure, which appears broadly comparable to that of other critically ill populations. While evidence specific to AKI is limited, protein provision of approximately 1.2-1.3 g/kg/day is generally recommended during critical illness. However, higher intakes of up to 1.7-2.5 g/kg/day may be considered in patients receiving RRT to offset extracorporeal amino acid losses and increased protein catabolism. In this setting, emerging concepts such as metabolic tolerance and biomarker-guided metabolic phenotyping may facilitate individualised nutritional strategies.

Conclusions: AKI, particularly when requiring RRT, is associated with profound and dynamic metabolic disturbances that substantially influence energy and protein requirements, thereby making nutrition an integral component of organ support therapies. Future research should evaluate precision nutrition strategies that tailor nutritional support to the phase of critical illness, measured energy expenditure, metabolic tolerance, and RRT-related nutrient losses and gains. Such studies should prioritise patient-centred outcomes, including physical function and recovery, in addition to nutritional and metabolic endpoints.
